html:
The political revolution of 1868 that ended the rule of the Tokugawa shogunate and put power back, in name, in the hands of the emperor, the young Emperor Meiji. It began a fast, state-led drive to modernise Japan along Western lines.

The crisis began in 1853, when Commodore Perry arrived with American warships and forced Japan to open its ports. The unequal treaties that followed made the shogunate look weak. Young samurai from the southwestern domains of Satsuma and Choshu, under the slogan "revere the emperor, expel the barbarians", turned against it. In January 1868 they took the palace in Kyoto and declared imperial rule restored. The Boshin War against Tokugawa loyalists followed and ended in 1869.

The new leaders soon dropped "expel the barbarians" and chose to learn from the West instead. In a few decades they:

  • Abolished the domains in 1871 and replaced them with prefectures run from Tokyo.
  • Ended the samurai class, its stipends and its right to carry swords.
  • Brought in conscription, a land tax paid in money and universal schooling.
  • Sent the Iwakura Mission to study America and Europe, and hired foreign experts.
  • Built railways, mills and banks, and wrote the Meiji Constitution of 1889.

Not everyone agreed. Former samurai rebelled, most famously in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, and were crushed by the new army. Thinkers such as Fukuzawa Yukichi spread Western ideas. Within forty years Japan had become an industrial power and an empire, the path of modern Japan.
sum: The political revolution of 1868 that ended the rule of the Tokugawa shogunate and put power back, in name, in the hands of the emperor, the young Emperor Meiji. It began a fast, state-led drive to modernise Japan along Western lines.
